title: NovaDocs Case Study Outline (Draft) — embeddings + reranking cost optimization
body:
NOTE: Draft outline + rough narrative for internal alignment. This is NOT customer-approved. Do not share externally.

Working angle / one-liner
- “NovaDocs cut retrieval cost per query while improving p95 latency by standardizing embeddings + reranking on Redwood Inference.”
- Primary positioning: Production economics (cost per query, predictable latency) for a high-volume SaaS doc search workload.
- Secondary positioning: Operational simplicity (versioning/rollouts, observability) + reliability (fallback options).

Customer snapshot (fill in once confirmed)
- Company: NovaDocs (SaaS — document search / knowledge retrieval for B2B teams)
- Buyer/user: Engineering + ML (search relevance) team
- Deployment: Redwood Hosted API (plus Redwood Console + Redwood Optimize)
- Workload type:
  - Embeddings for indexing + query embedding
  - Reranking top-K results for quality
  - Some “answer synthesis” may exist, but keep the story focused on embeddings + reranking economics unless they want broader scope
- Approx scale (placeholders):
  - Queries/day: [TBD]
  - Docs indexed: [TBD]
  - Average query length: [TBD]
  - Top-K retrieved before rerank: [TBD]

Target audience + where this will be used
- Audience:
  - AI product engineers building search/retrieval features
  - Platform teams standardizing inference endpoints
  - Buyers sensitive to unit economics (usage-based pricing pressures)
- Use cases:
  - Sales: proof point for “cost-per-query improvements with caching/batching + right model selection”
  - PLG: website case study page + PDF; link from quickstarts (“Customer stories”)
  - CS: reference profile for future calls on search workloads

Proposed headline + subhead (draft copy)
Option A (economics-forward)
- Headline: “NovaDocs reduced retrieval cost per query with Redwood Optimize”
- Subhead: “By tuning caching, batching, and model selection for embeddings + reranking, NovaDocs improved p95 latency and lowered inference spend while maintaining relevance quality.”

Option B (performance-forward)
- Headline: “NovaDocs scaled doc search to high-volume traffic with predictable latency”
- Subhead: “Redwood’s hosted inference and observability helped NovaDocs stabilize p95 and reduce cost with workload-aware optimizations.”

Key outcomes (must be quantified; placeholders for now)
We should pick 2–4 metrics max and be strict about measurement notes.
- Cost:
  - Cost per query down by [X%] (or $/1k queries down by [X%])
  - Monthly inference spend down by [$X] (optional; only if they’re comfortable)
- Latency:
  - p95 end-to-end retrieval latency down from [A ms] to [B ms] (or stabilized under [SLO])
  - Rerank stage latency p95 down [A→B]
- Reliability:
  - Error rate reduced from [A%] to [B%] (timeouts/429s)
  - Fewer incidents related to inference capacity: [TBD wording]
- Quality guardrail:
  - Relevance metric maintained or improved (e.g., NDCG@10, MRR, human eval pass rate) [TBD]

IMPORTANT: We need to be careful about attributing relevance improvements. If quality didn’t improve, we can position as “maintained quality while reducing cost” (often stronger/cleaner).

Narrative structure (web + PDF)
1) Problem
- NovaDocs’ doc search product usage grew (seat expansion + more content indexed), increasing inference volume.
- Their previous setup made cost unpredictable (per-query costs creeping up, reranker expensive), and performance varied at peak.
- Internal pressure: keep search fast and relevant without doubling inference spend.

2) Constraints / Requirements (make these feel real)
- Tight latency SLO for interactive search UX (p95 target) — [TBD actual]
- Cost sensitivity due to usage-based pricing and gross margin targets
- Need safe rollouts for model updates (no relevance regressions)
- Minimal infra overhead for the team (small ML/platform footprint)

3) Why Redwood (decision rationale)
- Needed a hosted inference option with:
  - transparent cost/latency breakdowns
  - knobs for caching/batching without rewriting their pipeline
  - ability to pin versions and run controlled rollouts
- Redwood’s differentiator to emphasize for this story:
  - Optimize recommendations tied to workload characteristics (sequence lengths, request distribution)
  - Console visibility into token/latency hotspots (even for non-generation endpoints, we can talk about request latency + throughput + error analysis)
  - Smart routing/fallback policies (if used, otherwise keep minimal)

4) Architecture (high-level, publishable)
We should include a simple diagram later; for now describe components.
- “Before” (likely):
  - Query → embed → vector DB top-K → reranker → results
  - Embeddings and reranking potentially split across vendors/self-hosted endpoints
  - Limited observability on per-stage latency/cost
- “After” (with Redwood):
  - Query embedding via Redwood Hosted API (embeddings endpoint)
  - Reranking via Redwood rerank endpoint (or text generation used as reranker if that’s what they do — confirm)
  - Redwood Console dashboards for route/model performance
  - Optimize-guided config changes:
    - caching (prefix/KV where applicable; for embeddings specifically, consider “query/result caching” at app layer and Redwood-side caching if supported)
    - batching (continuous batching / micro-batching where possible)
    - right-sizing model choice (smaller embedding model for queries, or separate models for indexing vs queries)

TODO: confirm what parts are truly Redwood-native vs app-layer. We should not claim token-level caching for embeddings unless we can describe it accurately.

5) Implementation details (what they actually did)
Keep this as “3–6 steps” so it reads like a playbook.
Draft steps:
- Step 1: Baseline + instrumentation
  - Defined measurement window: [e.g., 14 days], split by peak vs non-peak
  - Captured baseline p50/p95 latency and cost per query for:
    - query embedding
    - reranking
  - Identified tail latency drivers (timeouts, burst traffic, cold caches)
- Step 2: Model + endpoint standardization
  - Consolidated embedding + reranking endpoints on Redwood (reduced vendor sprawl)
  - Pinned model versions for repeatable evaluation
- Step 3: Apply Optimize recommendations
  - Batching: tuned batch sizes / concurrency limits to improve throughput while keeping p95 within SLO
  - Caching: added request/result caching where it made sense (e.g., repeated queries, common filters) + reduced redundant embedding calls
  - Routing policy: configured fallback to a compatible model variant during peak capacity events (ONLY if true)
- Step 4: Quality guardrails + rollouts
  - Ran A/B tests / canary on a subset of traffic
  - Used regression checks on a prompt set / query set (their relevance eval harness) [TBD]
- Step 5: Operationalize
  - Dashboards + alerts (latency, error rates)
  - Monthly/quarterly review cadence to revisit unit economics as product usage shifts

6) Results (quantified)
We’ll need a clean before/after table and 1–2 charts (web + PDF).
Draft table (placeholders):
- Metric | Before | After | Notes
- Cost per 1k queries | $[TBD] | $[TBD] | Same query mix; excludes vector DB costs
- Rerank p95 latency | [TBD] ms | [TBD] ms | Measured at application boundary
- Error rate (timeouts/429s) | [TBD]% | [TBD]% | Peak window 9am–12pm PT
- Quality (NDCG@10 or MRR) | [TBD] | [TBD] | No statistically significant regression

Measurement notes (required for credibility)
- Define “cost per query” explicitly:
  - Include which components: embeddings + rerank inference only
  - Exclude storage/vector DB, app compute, etc.
  - Define tokenization assumptions if reranking uses a generative model
- Latency definitions:
  - End-to-end retrieval latency = query received → final ranked results returned
  - Also report stage latencies if we have them (embedding call time, rerank call time)
- Ensure apples-to-apples:
  - Same K for rerank (e.g., rerank top 50)
  - Same query distribution and filters
  - Same region

Proof artifacts we should ask NovaDocs for (internal only)
- Screenshot exports from Redwood Console for:
  - route latency p50/p95 over time
  - throughput (RPS) during peak
  - error rate trend
- Their own app metrics dashboard confirming end-to-end latency + user impact
- Cost report view (even if anonymized: percentage changes + methodology)
- If they have eval results: a one-slide summary (metric name, sample size, confidence)

Customer quotes (draft placeholders; do not use until approved)
We should target 2 quotes: 1 technical, 1 business.
- Engineering quote (champion):
  - “We didn’t want to rebuild our retrieval stack just to get cost under control. Redwood gave us clear levers—batching and caching guidance—and the visibility to prove the impact.”
- Business/product quote:
  - “Search is core to our product. We needed to keep results fast as usage scaled without letting inference costs balloon.”

Open questions / TBDs for next interview
- Confirm exact endpoints/models used:
  - Embedding model(s) for indexing vs queries (same or different?)
  - Reranking approach (dedicated reranker model vs LLM-based rerank)
- Confirm caching story:
  - What is cached (query embeddings? full rerank results? prefix caching not relevant?)
  - Where caching happens (their service vs Redwood platform)
  - Cache hit rate and impact on cost/latency
- Confirm batching story:
  - Was batching applied via Redwood runtime automatically or through client-side concurrency settings?
  - What changed in practice (before/after configs)
- Confirm rollout/quality:
  - Did they run canary? A/B? shadow traffic?
  - What eval set did they use (size, time period)?
- Confirm what they’re willing to publish:
  - Company name/logo
  - Architecture diagram detail level
  - Numbers (absolute vs %)
  - Any mention of their vector DB vendor (likely avoid)

Risks / watch-outs (for Legal + Security + accuracy)
- Do not imply Redwood controls their vector database performance or relevance beyond the inference components.
- Be explicit about what costs are included; avoid “cut costs by X%” without defining the denominator.
- Avoid over-generalizing: outcomes are workload-specific (query mix, K, doc sizes, region).
- If they experienced any incident during onboarding/POC, make sure we don’t inadvertently contradict support history.

Draft outline for the final asset (web page)
- Hero: headline + 2–3 outcome callouts
- Customer snapshot (industry, size range, use case)
- Challenge
- Solution (architecture + implementation steps)
- Results (table + short narrative)
- Why it mattered (tie back to business)
- What’s next (optional: planned expansion, e.g., more reranking traffic, multi-region)
- CTA: “Talk to us” + “See docs”

Distribution plan (GTM notes)
- Publish target: align with case-studies section launch (ENG-4921)
- Add to:
  - Docs site case studies
  - Quickstarts README “Customer stories”
  - Sales enablement: one-page summary + reference profile
  - Optional: short blog post or benchmark-style snippet (only if NovaDocs open to it)

Next steps / action items
- Ethan (writer): schedule 45-min interview with NovaDocs (eng lead + product/ops) — focus on measurement rigor + what can be shared publicly
- Markus/Simran (SE): validate technical claims (batching/caching specifics, model/versioning language)
- Miguel/Rachel (CS): confirm reference readiness + boundaries for reference calls (frequency, topics)
- Soojin (PMM): finalize messaging angle and acceptable claim language
- Ben (Growth): align on publish slot + SEO keywords ("embeddings", "reranking", "cost per query")

Appendix: interview prompts (quick list)
- What broke first as usage grew: cost, latency, reliability, or quality?
- What did “good” look like (SLO + budget)?
- What did you change specifically (configs, caching policy, batching/concurrency, model choice)?
- How did you validate impact (window, sample size, dashboards)?
- What would you tell another team shipping doc search today?
